(a) Sheltered: supported. The article places a full, generator-powered ICU with 'medically fragile patients' at Earl K. (b) Forced movement: supported and explicit - 'the remaining 52 patients had to be evacuated' and 'ultimately evacuated all of its patients.' Note that 'the remaining 52' implies earlier transfers had already occurred, so 52 is the tail of the movement, not the total.

(c) Mechanism: supported and explicit - a compound failure. First, generators that ran clinical equipment but not air conditioning in a sealed building ('the vast majority of those generators couldn't power air conditioning systems, a critical flaw in modern American hospitals built with sealed windows and filled with heat-producing electrical equipment'), producing an ICU so hot that 'None of the staff could find a thermometer that went up high enough.' Then the failed attempt to rejoin the grid: smoke, a failed switch. Regional utility loss is documented in the same article ('Well over half a million business and home customers in the region were still without electricity on Friday afternoon').

The source dates its ICU observation to Wednesday Sept 3 and describes one patient being taken down the elevator during that visit, which is the basis for evac_start_best = 2008-09-03; that inference is reasonable. But the source never says when the evacuation began or when the switch failed, and its narrative window extends to Friday Sept 5. RECOMMENDATION: widen evac_start_hi from 2008-09-04 to 2008-09-05 and keep precision = 'approximate'. The lo bound of 2008-09-03 is defensible because patients were demonstrably still in-house that day.

OVER-READING IN THE REGISTRY NARRATIVE: the 'detail' field states 'all remaining 52 patients were evacuated via the single working elevator.' The article says only that 'An ambulance crew took ONE of them down the hospital's single working elevator.' Attributing all 52 movements to that elevator is an inference beyond the source and should be softened (e.g. 'moved out via the hospital's single working elevator' or drop the elevator claim from the 52-patient sentence).

Checked and rejected: LSU Health's own hurricane page for EKLMC (https://www.lsuhospitals.org/hurricanes/ekl.shtml) covers Katrina/Rita 2005 only and says nothing about Gustav; the Wikipedia entry for Earl K. Long Medical Center contains no hurricane or evacuation content; the MCEER Gustav reconnaissance report (08-SP07) covers New Orleans-area acute care hospitals only; the AP dispatches of Sept 2-3, 2008 describe the ~700-patient/dozen-hospital Baton Rouge-area problem but do not name Earl K. Action: keep the POST_FSIP label, retain MEDIUM (or lower to MEDIUM-LOW) confidence, widen the upper date bound, correct the elevator sentence, and flag in the paper's limitations that this event rests on a single journalistic source.

notes:
FETCH STATUS: the Tampa Bay Times URL now returns only the headline and photo caption behind a subscriber wall, and the CNN URL returns HTTP 451 (Unavailable For Legal Reasons) to direct requests. Both were recovered in full from the Wayback Machine (tampabay snapshot 2016-11-08; CNN snapshot 2016-11-11, id_ raw capture) and are quoted from those captures. The Patch item fetched live. The registry should record the Wayback URLs alongside the live ones so the citations remain resolvable.

THE FACTS ARE SOLID; THE LABEL IS NOT.

(b) Forced movement: fully supported. 209 patients moved overnight Aug 31 - Sept 1; elevators out, so 'crews had to strap patients to stretchers and carry them down from the upper floors'; more than 70 ambulances and three ambulance buses from as far as Orlando; ICU and critical patients first; receiving hospitals enumerated (Oak Hill 49, Medical Center of Trinity 31, Northside 26, Memorial Hospital of Tampa 26, plus Morton Plant North Bay, St. Petersburg General, Brandon Regional).

(c) Mechanism: fully supported and more specific than the CNN account. Per CEO Shayne George in the Tampa Bay Times, lightning struck the roof about 6:15 p.m., started a roofline fire that damaged the electrical system and killed the power; when the emergency generators came on, 'electricity flowed through the damaged wiring... causing a safety issue,' so staff had to shut the backup power OFF. CNN, by contrast, calls it simply 'an electrical fire' in 'the generator room' and does not mention lightning or the storm at all - hence its 'partial' rating. Note the registry's 'generator-room/roof fire' phrasing merges two different source accounts; the Times (with the CEO on record) says roofline, CNN says generator room.

(d) Date: fully supported and exact.

(a) SHELTERED: NOT SUPPORTED - THE SOURCES SHOW THE OPPOSITE. The hospital did not shelter through Hermine. It was completely emptied of patients on Aug 31 - Sept 1 and, per the Times, 'won't readmit patients until Monday at the earliest' (it in fact resumed operations the following Tuesday). Hermine made landfall as a Category 1 hurricane near St. Marks, FL in the early hours of Sept 2 - about 150 miles north of Hudson and roughly a day AFTER the last patient left. The hospital's census at landfall was zero. Under the registry's stated POST_FSIP definition ('sheltered then forced to move patients AFTER storm conditions arrived because operations broke down'), the 'sheltered' element fails outright.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE REGISTRY ITSELF: the row is coded POST_FSIP with confidence HIGH, yet its own 'detail' field concedes 'evacuation occurred before landfall (Sept 2 at St. Marks).' A reviewer will catch this. It must be resolved before publication.

THE ONE ARGUMENT FOR THE CURRENT LABEL, stated fairly: the Times does place the trigger inside the storm's envelope - lightning struck 'while the storm that would become Hurricane Hermine was lashing the region,' and staff evacuated 'while a tropical storm approached.' Hermine was upgraded to a named tropical storm only that same Wednesday afternoon (Patch: 'upgraded to a named storm early Wednesday afternoon'). So storm-related weather had arrived even though the storm itself had not. If the registry's FSIP construct keys on 'storm conditions arrived' in the loosest sense rather than on impact/landfall, a case can be made. But the hospital never attempted to ride out the storm with patients in the building, which is the causal phenomenon the FSIP category is meant to capture, and treating a ~36-hour-pre-landfall full evacuation as a failed shelter-in-place will distort any timing analysis (this event's evac_start sits far to the left of every genuine post-impact case and will act as a leverage point).

RECOMMENDATION: relabel. Move E006 out of primary_FSIP to a pre-landfall / storm-adjacent infrastructure-failure evacuation category (i.e. a peripheral-hazard evacuation completed before storm impact), or exclude it from the FSIP analytic set and report it as a sensitivity case. If the authors instead elect to keep it, the label must be re-documented explicitly ('storm conditions present, pre-landfall'), confidence dropped from HIGH to at most MEDIUM, and the event excluded from or separately flagged in any post-landfall timing distribution.

MINOR DISCREPANCY FOR THE RECORD: HCA's own 2017 retrospective (recorded as additional_source) says 'Of the 225 patients evacuated, 40 were in intensive care units' and 'More than 150 patients were transferred to 13 other hospitals,' against the contemporaneous 209 figure used by the Times, CNN and the registry. The contemporaneous figure is the better one to publish; note the discrepancy if the count is reported. HCA also confirms the mechanism independently: 'lightning began a roof fire, which in turn knocked out the facility's power.'

notes: THE POST_FSIP LABEL IS CONTRADICTED BY THE SOURCES. Every source that states a date places the patient movement BEFORE storm conditions reached Houston, as a precautionary pre-landfall evacuation, not a forced post-storm one. The Houston Chronicle story published the evening of Fri Aug 25, 2017 - before Harvey's ~10 pm CDT landfall at Rockport - already reports in the past tense that East Houston Regional 'suspended all operations and evacuated its patients Friday morning as Hurricane Harvey barreled closer to the Texas coast,' and that 51 patients had been transferred to other HCA Gulf Coast facilities, some as far as Conroe, 'to consolidate resources and for patient safety purposes.' The Chronicle's Nov 10, 2017 closure story states the hospital 'made the early decision to evacuate all 80 patients and cease operations on Aug. 25' because of its proximity to Greens Bayou and its flood-prone history; HealthExec (Nov 10, 2017) says the same, explicitly 'ahead of Harvey making landfall.' None of the four cited sources describes any patient being moved after storm conditions arrived. Recommended action: relabel - remove E009 from the primary_FSIP group and code it as a pre-landfall / pre-emptive evacuation. It should NOT be recoded SIP_OK either, because the hospital did not shelter in place; with only POST_FSIP and SIP_OK available in this registry's vocabulary, the event should be excluded from the shelter-in-place cohort entirely, or a pre-emptive-evacuation category added. Consequences for the adjudicated timing: evac_start_best 2017-08-27 and the lo bound 2017-08-25 are both wrong for a forced movement - the actual movement date is 2017-08-25 (Friday morning), and there is no forced post-storm movement to date. The registry narrative's own hedge ('Timing of the patient movement (at storm onset vs. during peak flooding) is inconsistently reported') resolves cleanly against the FSIP reading once the Aug 25 Chronicle piece is read. What IS true and well sourced is the facility damage: floodgates installed after Tropical Storm Allison were overtopped, roughly six feet of water entered the 131-bed hospital, and HCA announced in Nov 2017 that it would never reopen (479 employees laid off, 'well over 400' reassigned) - the only Texas hospital permanently closed by Harvey. That is a facility-damage/closure event, not a failed shelter-in-place. Also note a patient-count discrepancy across sources (51 transferred per the Aug 25 Chronicle vs. 'all 80 patients' per the Nov 2017 Chronicle and HealthExec). SEPARATE DATA-QUALITY DEFECT: E009 carries ccn 450097 and cohort_name 'BAYSHORE MEDICAL CENTER', identical to E008. East Houston Regional Medical Center is a distinct HCA Gulf Coast facility with its own CCN; the CMS linkage on this row is wrong and must be fixed or the row dropped, otherwise E008 and E009 double-count the same provider number. Fetch notes: healthexec.com and fiercehealthcare.com return 403 to WebFetch; the HealthExec article has also been moved from the cited /topics/care-delivery/ path to /topics/patient-care/precision-medicine/houston-hospital-closing-after-hurricane-damage - text confirmed from Wayback snapshot 20251012112123 (John Gregory, Nov 10, 2017). The FierceHealthcare item (Paige Minemyer, Nov 13, 2017) was read from a Wayback snapshot; note its cited URL slug contains 'tenet-healthcare' although East Houston Regional was an HCA facility (Tenet appears only in an unrelated earnings paragraph). abc13.com fetched live (Nov 12, 2017) but contains no evacuation timing at all.

NPR (Aug 30) is the weakest of the four - it confirms a 'Ben Taub decision to evacuate' and the food shortage in an interview with SETRAC's Darrell Pile, and its editor's note says Ben Taub had reopened, but it gives no dates or patient counts; keep it as corroboration only. The registry's only citation is the hospital's own retrospective marketing page, whose 'never closed its doors' claim is, on the contemporaneous record, true only of the EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT. I located three independent sources the row does not cite, and they materially complicate the SIP_OK label. WHAT IS NOW SUPPORTED: the hospital did not evacuate before landfall and was still functioning on site afterward - WJHG's Calhoun County status report (published Oct. 22, 2018; hospital line carried in the Oct. 24, 2018 update) states it was 'on generator power with an open Emergency Department', and its damage narrative (roof torn off, windows smashed, ongoing water intrusion) is only consistent with the building being occupied and operating through the storm. That supports the 'sheltered' half of SIP_OK, though no source describes the facility's status on Oct 10 itself, so I grade it partial rather than yes. WHAT IS NOT SUPPORTED - AND THIS IS THE REASON I RECOMMEND REVIEW: SIP_OK requires the hospital to be 'documented as operating without forced patient movement', and no source documents that. The opposite-leaning evidence is affirmative and from two independent outlets. WJHG (Nov. 16, 2018): 'The storm tore off the hospital's roof, smashed windows, and while the emergency room remains open, the hospital remains closed to inpatients with no reopening in sight', and 'Patients needing hospital care in the Blountstown area are being sent to Dothan or Tallahassee.' Tallahassee Democrat (Jul. 19, 2019): 'It wasn't until this spring that the hospital reopened inpatient services', with '80 percent of its roof ... peeled away' and the main lobby and lab 'forced to close and relocate'; bed count fell from 25 to 10. So this 25-bed critical access hospital's inpatient unit ceased functioning at the storm and stayed shut for roughly five to six months. If ANY inpatients were on census when Michael struck on Oct 10, 2018, they necessarily had to be moved out afterward - which is precisely the POST_FSIP pattern (sheltered, then patients forced out because operations broke down). No source I could reach states the Oct 10-11 inpatient census or what became of those patients; the Tallahassee Democrat feature, which is the most detailed retrospective available, describes the storm damage at length and never mentions an evacuation or transfer either way. RECOMMENDED RESOLUTION: do not keep this row as a clean SIP_OK on the current basis. Obtain the Oct 10, 2018 inpatient census / discharge-transfer records (Florida AHCA emergency status reporting, the hospital's own CMS cost report or Medicare claims for transfers dated Oct 10-15, 2018, or a direct statement from hospital administration). If the census was zero at landfall (plausible for a 25-bed CAH that had days of warning and may have discharged down), SIP_OK is defensible but should be re-cited to the WJHG Oct 2018 status report rather than the hospital's About page, and the detail field should be corrected to say the ED stayed open while inpatient services were lost. If any inpatients were transferred out post-landfall, relabel to POST_FSIP with evac_start on or about 2018-10-10/11. Either way the current LOW confidence should stand or drop until that is settled. CAVEAT ON observed_through: I set it to 2018-10-24, the latest date on which a source shows the facility operating on site. Be aware this is ED-only operation; it is not evidence that no inpatient transfer occurred, and it should not be read as such in the paper. LATER FORCED EVACUATION: none found. The facility limped on and was ultimately replaced - FEMA approved roughly $11.4 million in 2020 and a new $47 million hospital opened in July/August 2025 - but that is a rebuild, not a storm evacuation.

SOURCE CHAIN. The single cited URL is a Florida Trend health-care news roundup (dated 9/12/2017), not a reported article. Its entire Broward Health North content is a two-sentence aggregator blurb of a Denver7 (KMGH) story: "Downed trees, heavy winds and torrential rain are among the images capturing a glimpse of Irma passing over Broward Health North hospital in Florida. Denver native Matthew Smedberg has been calling the hospital home." I traced and retrieved the underlying Denver7 article from the Wayback Machine (capture 2017-09-11 16:53 GMT; byline timestamp 7:53 AM, Sep 11, 2017) and record it as additional_source.

WHAT THE SOURCES ACTUALLY SHOW. The Denver7 piece is an interview with Matthew Smedberg, an HSS Security contractor from Denver who was training staff at Broward Health North and rode out the storm there, taking over the hospital's safety and security operations. It establishes: (i) the hospital went into lockdown the morning of Sep 10 and was occupied and staffed while Irma passed over — i.e., no pre-landfall closure/relocation of operations; (ii) no evacuation or patient transfer is mentioned anywhere; (iii) the hospital lost utility power when the hurricane hit; and (iv) there were "a couple of little fires" inside the hospital from water intrusion and electrical damage. The Florida Trend blurb adds nothing beyond the first sentence.

WHY ONLY 'PARTIAL' ON sheltered_supported. Skeptically read, neither source ever mentions patients, census, admissions, or operating status. They document staff/security presence and building conditions during the storm, not that inpatients remained in the building or that the hospital continued clinical operations. A facility that had moved patients out pre-landfall could equally have had a ride-out security team on site. So the absence of a pre-landfall evacuation is strongly implied (hospital in hurricane lockdown, contractor sheltering inside, storm passing over) but is nowhere stated, and 'stayed open' is not stated by any source at all.

REGISTRY DETAIL OVER-READS THE SOURCE. The abstracted detail says "Sheltered in place and stayed open through heavy winds, downed trees and torrential rain." The "downed trees, heavy winds and torrential rain" clause is lifted from the blurb, but "stayed open" is an inference not supported by the cited text. Recommend softening the detail field to what the source supports (occupied and in lockdown through the storm) or citing the Denver7 original directly.

ADVERSE SIGNAL WORTH RECORDING. The Denver7 story documents loss of utility power at the hospital during Irma plus water intrusion causing small internal electrical fires. That is real infrastructure degradation of exactly the kind that drives POST_FSIP events elsewhere in the registry. It does not by itself defeat SIP_OK — there is no evidence of any forced patient movement, and generator backup is the expected response — but it means this facility was not an undisturbed shelter-in-place, and the coding rests on absence of evidence of transfer rather than on positive documentation of uninterrupted operation.

SEARCH FOR A LATER FORCED EVACUATION. I found none. WebSearch was unavailable (session search budget exhausted, 200/200) and Bing/DuckDuckGo/Brave/Ecosia/Mojeek all returned bot-detection or CAPTCHA pages, which I did not attempt to bypass. I substituted Google News RSS queries ("Broward Health North" Irma; "Broward Health" hurricane Irma evacuate; Broward hospitals Irma date-bounded 2017-09-10 to 2017-09-20) and the Wayback CDX API. Nothing surfaced any Broward Health North evacuation or patient transfer. The prominent post-Irma South Florida forced-movement story in those results is the Rehabilitation Center at Hollywood Hills nursing home (patients moved to Memorial Regional Hospital) — a different, non-Broward Health facility, so it is not a contradiction here. The Wayback capture of browardhealth.org from 2017-09-13 shows a stale homepage with no Irma status statement and is recorded only to document that this avenue was checked.

BOTTOM LINE. SIP_OK is the most plausible label and nothing contradicts it, but the evidence base is one two-sentence aggregator blurb plus its underlying human-interest TV story that never mentions patients. observed_through is set to 2017-09-11 (the Denver7 publication date, the day after Irma's Broward-area conditions), which is the last date on which a source shows the hospital occupied and running its own operations with no transfer reported. Keep at reduced confidence (the row's MEDIUM confidence is, if anything, generous), and ideally add a corroborating source that positively documents patients/operations — e.g., a Broward Health or AHCA post-Irma facility-status statement, or Sun Sentinel/WPLG/NBC6 coverage of which Broward hospitals remained open — before this event carries weight in the analysis.
